report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by high-quality evidence. Studies that compare vaccinated children with appropriate controls, rather than simply noting that autism diagnoses and vaccination schedules both changed over time, do not find that more childhood vaccination causes autism.

Most directly, a study measured each child’s *total vaccine-antigen exposure* from records during the first two years of life and found no association with autism risk: https://www.jpeds.com/article/s0022-3476(13)00144-3/fulltext

A meta-analysis likewise found no association between autism and vaccination, MMR, thimerosal/mercury, or multiple vaccines: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367

The often-cited MMR concern has also been tested in a nationwide Danish cohort of 657,461 children; it examined autism risk overall, in higher-risk subgroups, and after vaccination, and found no increased risk: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30831578/

An independent National Academies review concluded that epidemiologic evidence favored rejecting a causal relationship between MMR or thimerosal-containing vaccines and autism: https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/10997

The view can seem plausible because vaccine visits occur during the same developmental period when autism traits often become noticeable and diagnoses are made. But timing alone cannot establish causation; it can reflect detection, changing diagnostic practices, and other differences between children. The relevant evidence is therefore the controlled cohort, case-control, and review literature above—and it does not show that increasing the number of childhood vaccines increases autism.
